pages.title: Speech errors as linguistic evidence
pages.c: **Speech errors reveal how an utterance is planned.** An error can separate parts of a word, move a sound into another position, or replace an intended word with a related one. The form of the error provides evidence about the units that the production system represents and the processes that organize them.
support: Fromkin’s title “Speech errors as linguistic evidence” takes errors seriously as a source of knowledge about language. If linguistic competence is studied separately from the disruptions of performance, an error might be set aside. Examining its structure instead makes performance informative about the organization of the system.
The useful question is why this particular error occurred. A theory should explain which elements were active, what was selected, and how the produced form differs from the intended one.
pages.d: An occasional error can expose a distinction that fluent speech conceals. When the intended and produced forms are compared, the part that changed and the parts that remained stable help identify what the system was doing.

pages.title: Spreading activation and competing candidates
pages.c: **Spreading activation explains why an unintended item can become available during speech planning.** Words and other representations activate related items. Similarity can concern meaning, grammatical properties, or sound. The intended item therefore competes with alternatives that may receive activation from several sources at once.
support: Frequency affects how readily an item becomes active. Common words are generally easier to activate than uncommon words, so the amount of activation required to produce a particular candidate differs across items.

Recently spoken material remains active, and material planned for an upcoming part of the utterance is already becoming active. Other thoughts can contribute activation as well. “Noise” includes fluctuations and interference within this system, rather than referring only to sounds in the environment.
pages.d: A production error becomes understandable when the activation of a competitor is traced. It may resemble the intended item, have been spoken a moment ago, or be waiting to be spoken. These influences can combine, allowing an unintended candidate to enter the utterance.

pages.title: Tip-of-the-tongue states and phonological priming
pages.c: **A tip-of-the-tongue state involves partial activation without successful production of the target word.** A person can recognize the intended meaning while failing to retrieve enough of its sound form to say it. In a spreading-activation account, a related prime can increase activation of the missing form and help it reach the level required for production.
support: In the example reviewed by Lise Abrams, a definition asks for goods traded illegally. The target is “contraband.” People experiencing a tip-of-the-tongue state read words that overlap with the target’s first, middle, or final syllable, or words without the relevant overlap, before attempting the target again.

Resolution is highest after first-syllable primes such as “contact,” “connotation,” and “conscious.” The result connects recovery with the location of sound overlap. The frequency principle also predicts greater retrieval difficulty for less accessible words, whose forms are harder to activate.
pages.d: The participant already has a target meaning in mind. The prime supplies related phonological activation rather than a new definition of the answer. Comparing the overlap conditions therefore helps identify which sound information is useful in recovering a partially available word.
pages.visual: The four bars compare first-syllable, middle-syllable, final-syllable, and unrelated-word conditions. First-syllable priming produces about 50 percent resolution, compared with roughly one-quarter for the unrelated condition. Middle-syllable overlap is intermediate, while final-syllable overlap is close to the unrelated condition.

pages.title: Anticipation, perseveration, and sound exchanges
pages.c: **Slips of the tongue differ in the direction that a sound moves.** In anticipation, a sound planned for later appears too soon. In perseveration, an earlier sound carries into a later position. In metathesis or exchange, elements trade positions within the utterance. Comparing the intended and produced forms identifies the pattern.
support: “Week long race” becoming “reek long race” is anticipation because the upcoming r replaces the beginning of “week.” “John gave the boy” becoming “John gave the goy” is perseveration because the earlier g carries into “boy.”

“Keep a tape” becoming “teep a cape” is an exchange. The initial k and t trade positions while the remaining parts of the two words remain in place. The classification concerns the relation between the two forms, not whether the resulting expression makes sense.
pages.d: The order of the intended sounds is essential. The same kind of sound substitution can reflect a later item arriving early or an earlier item persisting. An exchange has the further property that both displaced elements appear in each other’s positions.
pages.visual: The examples align intended and produced expressions. In “keep a tape” and “teep a cape,” the changed initial consonants reveal the exchange. In the anticipation and perseveration examples, only one position changes, and the source of that replacement is respectively later or earlier in the utterance.

pages.title: Explaining the direction of a speech error
pages.c: **The direction of a slip identifies a likely source of competing activation.** Anticipation fits the activation of material that is being prepared for an upcoming position. Perseveration fits the continued activation of material that has just been spoken. An exchange reveals interference between elements being organized within the same planned utterance.
support: In “week long race” becoming “reek long race,” the r is available before its intended position. In “John gave the boy” becoming “John gave the goy,” the g remains influential after its own position. Both patterns follow from planning that extends beyond the sound currently being articulated.

Similarity and frequency affect which candidates compete effectively, while fluctuations in activation can affect which one is selected. A particular error gives especially clear evidence about the items participating in that competition.
pages.d: Preparing an utterance requires several elements to be active around the same time. This overlap supports fluent production, because the speaker can prepare what comes next while speaking. It also creates an opportunity for the wrong active element to be selected for a position.
pages.visual: The repeated examples support a different comparison here. Their temporal order distinguishes activation from a future part of the plan from activation left over from a past part. The exchange examples show two elements interfering with their assignment to positions.

pages.title: Mondegreens and word boundaries
pages.c: **A mondegreen is a misheard expression produced by interpreting the speech signal differently from what the speaker intended.** The name comes from hearing “laid him on the green” as “Lady Mondegreen.” The listener assigns the sounds to a different sequence of words, changing the interpreted message.
support: Speech arrives continuously, so word boundaries must be inferred. “The good candy came anyways” and “The good can decay many ways” illustrate how similar stretches of sound can be grouped into different words. Context helps choose among interpretations.

Songs can make this task especially difficult because their rhythm and melody change the usefulness of ordinary prosodic cues. “Hold me closer, Tony Danza” is a mishearing of “Hold me closer, tiny dancer.” The error belongs to perception rather than to the singer’s word selection.
pages.d: The listener’s task includes deciding both which sounds occurred and where one word ends and another begins. A familiar name or plausible phrase can organize the incoming sound into a coherent but unintended interpretation.
pages.visual: “Laid him on the green” and “Lady Mondegreen” use different word boundaries and lexical identities. The Tiny Dancer example likewise replaces a descriptive phrase with a familiar name. The contrast is between the sung or spoken expression and the listener’s interpretation of it.

pages.title: Malapropisms and familiar-word interpretations
pages.c: **Some malapropisms develop when a listener interprets an unfamiliar word as a more familiar one.** Hearing “congenital” and interpreting it as “congenial” can lead someone to say “a congenial heart defect.” At that point the speaker may be producing exactly the expression they intend, even though that expression arose from a mistaken interpretation.
support: This is a top-down influence on perception. An available lexical candidate helps organize the heard sound, and a similar familiar word can win over a less familiar target. The resulting expression can then become the speaker’s own version of the phrase.

The distinction matters when classifying an error. An unintended slip during production and an intended repetition of a mislearned expression can sound equally odd, but they arise through different processes.
pages.d: “Congenital” concerns a condition present from birth, whereas “congenial” concerns a pleasing or compatible quality. Their similar sound supports the substitution even though their meanings differ. The example shows how familiarity can influence which lexical interpretation is accepted.
pages.visual: The collected examples place familiar-looking expressions into contexts where a different word was intended. “Congenial heart defect” is particularly revealing because the speaker can preserve a grammatical phrase while replacing the medical word with a similar-sounding familiar one.

pages.title: Consonant clusters and the units of planning
pages.c: **Speech errors show that individual consonants can be manipulated within a cluster.** Fromkin’s examples bear on whether planning treats a cluster as one indivisible unit or represents its component sounds. “Fish grotto” becoming “frish gotto” moves the r out of the gr cluster and places it after the initial f.
support: If the complete initial clusters moved together, the gr sequence would move intact to the first word and f would move to the second. The observed “frish gotto” instead separates r from g and joins r to the f already in the first word.

“Fresh clear water” becoming “flesh queer water” provides another example. The r and l exchange within clusters, while the initial f and k remain in their positions. These errors provide evidence for segment-sized units in production planning.
pages.d: The inference depends on the structure of the change. Both the original and erroneous expressions contain consonant clusters, but the cluster does not travel as a single block. A model must allow access to the individual segment that is moved or exchanged.
pages.visual: The intended-to-produced pairs identify the migrating segments. In “fish grotto” to “frish gotto,” r leaves gr and joins f. In “fresh clear water” to “flesh queer water,” r and l exchange while the first consonants of the clusters stay in place. Those are different outcomes from whole-cluster exchanges.

pages.title: From meaning to an articulated utterance
pages.c: **A production model explains how an intended meaning becomes an ordered sequence of speech movements.** Fromkin’s 1971 model separates the organization of meaning and sentence structure from lexical selection, sound specification, and the motor commands that produce an utterance. Different kinds of error can provide evidence about these intermediate representations.
support: The proposed process begins with meaning to be conveyed and develops syntactic and semantic structure. Intonation and lexical information contribute to a representation containing ordered segments, syllables, and linguistic features.

Morphophonemic and phonetic processes further specify the sound sequence before the resulting motor commands drive articulation. The model’s distinct representations make it possible for an error to affect one part of planning while other properties remain organized.
pages.d: A fluent utterance hides the work between having something to say and moving the speech organs. Representing these intervening steps lets a theory ask whether an error concerns the chosen word, its sound form, its position, or the commands that realize it.
pages.visual: The arrows run from meaning through syntactic and semantic structure toward phonetic specification and motor commands. The lexicon contributes lexical information partway through this process. The final box is the produced utterance, after the intermediate representations have been transformed into a fully specified speech sequence.

pages.title: Levels of speech production
pages.c: **The basic production model distinguishes message planning, functional planning, positional organization, phonological encoding, and speech gestures.** The message concerns what the speaker intends to convey. Functional planning selects lemmas and associates them with semantic roles. Further planning organizes the clause, specifies its sound structure, and prepares the gestures used to say it.
support: These distinctions separate aspects of production that ordinary use of the word “word” can blur together. Choosing a conceptually appropriate lexical item is different from selecting its grammatical form or assembling the sounds that will express it.

An error is informative when it helps distinguish these representations. A word can exchange with another while retaining the grammatical form required by its new position, or a sound can move while the intended sentence organization remains recognizable.
pages.d: The level names identify different problems within producing an utterance. The speaker has to determine a message, select linguistic material, arrange it, and realize it as speech. Describing those problems separately gives a framework for explaining why different errors have different structures.

pages.title: Message planning depends on the audience
pages.c: **Message planning determines what information the speaker intends to communicate.** Winning money on a Sunday football game could be described differently to a supporter of the losing team, someone uninterested in football, or a public audience reading a short post. The event stays the same, while the communicative purpose and selected information can change.
support: The supporter’s feelings may affect how directly the winning is emphasized. Someone uninterested in football may require a different explanation of why the event matters. A short written post creates another set of choices about which details to include.
This makes the message level difficult to specify experimentally. Providing the same event does not establish that every speaker intends exactly the same content for every listener.
pages.d: The message is more than a record of what happened. It reflects the information the speaker chooses to convey in a particular interaction. Audience, goals, and the assumed knowledge of the listener help determine that choice.

pages.title: Picture-book elicitation and intended messages
pages.c: **Picture-book elicitation gives speakers a shared event or scene to describe.** A researcher can use a book such as “Frog, where are you?” so that participants encounter the same visual material. Their descriptions can then be compared while the visible stimulus is held constant.
support: The image still permits different communicative choices. A speaker can focus on different characters, actions, or relations and can assume different knowledge in the audience. Age and culture may influence how a message is organized.

The experimental method controls what participants see more directly than it controls what they intend to say. Distinguishing the shared picture from the selected message is therefore essential when interpreting the resulting speech.
pages.d: A common picture gives the researcher a reference for comparing descriptions. It does not supply a complete linguistic message by itself. The participant still has to decide what is relevant about that scene and how it should be communicated to the listener.
pages.visual: The picture supplies a boy, a dog, and frogs as shared referents. Speakers can identify those entities yet choose different aspects of the scene for their descriptions. The visible referents provide common material while leaving message selection open.

pages.title: Lemma selection precedes grammatical form
pages.c: **A lemma represents a lexical identity before its final grammatical form is determined.** The intended expression “Where’d I put it when I brought it in” becomes “Where’d I bring it when I put it in.” The verbs exchange positions, but BRING is realized as “bring” in its new position rather than carrying the surface form “brought” with it.
support: The first clause already contains the past-tense auxiliary did in “Where’d.” The verb that follows it takes the base form, so the exchanged BRING appears as “bring.” This preserves the grammatical requirements of the new position.

An exchange of two fully formed words would instead move “brought” as an unchanged sound-and-form package. The actual error supports separating selection of the lemma BRING from the processes that determine its final expression.
pages.d: The crucial evidence is the combination of lexical movement and grammatical adjustment. BRING changes its place in the sentence plan, and its form is fitted to that new environment. PUT looks the same in its base and past forms, so BRING provides the visible evidence for the separation.
pages.visual: The two expressions keep their overall clause pattern while exchanging the verbs. Comparing “brought” in the intended second clause with “bring” after “Where’d I” in the produced first clause reveals that the exchange occurred before the final verb form was fixed.

pages.title: Selecting the opposite of the intended word
pages.c: **A lemma-selection error can replace an intended word with its opposite.** Saying “like” where “hate” was intended, or “hot” where “cold” was intended, changes the message substantially while preserving a familiar grammatical pattern. These substitutions are revealing because opposite meanings remain closely related within the lexical system.
support: “Top” and “bottom” describe contrasting positions within the same spatial relation. “Oral” and “written” identify contrasting forms of an examination. The alternative is relevant to the same domain even when it conveys the wrong member of the contrast.

The produced word can therefore be both semantically related to the intended item and sharply different in what it asserts. This combination makes antonym errors useful for examining lexical competition.
pages.d: An opposite is often a particularly available alternative. Thinking about one endpoint brings the contrasting endpoint into the same conceptual comparison. If the wrong candidate is selected, the sentence can remain well formed while the intended proposition is reversed.
pages.visual: The paired examples preserve surrounding grammatical material while replacing one lexical item. The contrasts involve the same kinds of things, such as temperature for “hot” and “cold” or examination format for “oral” and “written.”

pages.title: Why antonyms compete effectively
pages.c: **Antonyms receive activation through several kinds of overlap at once.** They are semantically related, strongly associated, and often members of the same word class. They can also occupy the same semantic and syntactic roles. These properties make an antonym a plausible competitor during lemma selection.
support: “Hot” and “cold” both describe temperature and can complete the same sentence frame. Activating the intended temperature concept can also activate the contrasting candidate. If the wrong candidate wins, the remaining production processes can still form an ordinary sentence around it.

This explains why a major change in meaning can accompany a small, grammatically smooth substitution. The competitor fits the structure because many of its lexical properties match those of the intended item.
pages.d: Semantic similarity here does not mean having the same meaning. It means sharing a domain and a close relation within that domain. Association supplies another route for activation to spread, while grammatical compatibility allows the selected alternative to pass into the utterance.

pages.title: Blends and competing word forms
pages.c: **A blend combines material from competing words in a single produced form.** Lewis Carroll’s “frumious” combines “fuming” and “furious” deliberately. Spontaneous blends provide a related kind of evidence because parts of more than one lexical alternative contribute to the output.
support: Fromkin distinguishes the literary construction from the ways spontaneous blends often join words. Shared sounds can provide points at which the material from the alternatives comes together. The relation between the source words and the produced form therefore matters as much as the unusual result.
A blend differs from replacing one whole word with another. It indicates that information from both alternatives entered the construction of the spoken form.
pages.d: Two candidates may express closely related intended meanings and become active together. A blend gives evidence that the competition was not completely resolved before aspects of their phonological forms affected the utterance.
pages.visual: The passage contrasts Carroll’s intentional “fuming” plus “furious” construction with phonological combinations predicted for spontaneous production. Its point concerns how the contributing word forms overlap, rather than treating every invented portmanteau as an observed speech error.

pages.title: Naturally occurring blends
pages.c: **Spontaneous blends reveal competition among alternative ways of expressing a message.** Competing alternatives include “mainly” with “mostly,” “bother” with “trouble,” and “player” with “athlete.” These alternatives overlap in meaning and can become active during the same act of lexical selection.
support: The produced “swindged” combines phonological material associated with SWITCH and CHANGE. A single word form contains contributions from two candidates, so the error differs from an exchange in which two complete items trade places.

Choosing among alternatives is an ordinary part of speaking. Blends make that competition visible because information from more than one candidate survives into the output, rather than one candidate being expressed cleanly.
pages.d: The inference connects meaning-level competition with sound-level consequences. Alternatives can be appropriate to a similar message, yet have different phonological forms. A blended output shows that those different forms were active closely enough to influence the same produced word.
pages.visual: The paired alternatives identify how the unfamiliar output was formed. “Swindged” combines material from the pair recorded as “switch/changed.” The other pairs, such as “mainly/mostly” and “bother/trouble,” identify candidates that offer similar ways of expressing a message.

pages.title: Semantic roles remain stable across sentence forms
pages.c: **Semantic roles identify how participants relate to an event.** In “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me,” the plums are the undergoer, the icebox supplies the location, and the speaker is the agent. “I have eaten the plums in the icebox” describes the same basic event with a different arrangement of those roles.
support: Functional planning can associate EAT with the event, the speaker with the agent role, and PLUM with the undergoer role before a final clause arrangement is produced. Active and passive structures place these participants in different grammatical positions.

The speaker appears as “I” in the active subject position and “me” after “by” in the passive expression. The stable semantic role and changing grammatical form distinguish event organization from its final sentence expression.
pages.d: Agent does not mean first noun phrase, and undergoer does not mean second noun phrase. The agent is the participant carrying out the eating, regardless of where that participant appears. Recognizing this stability makes it possible to compare different sentences that express the same event.
pages.visual: The passive sequence places undergoer and location before the verb and agent. The active sequence starts with agent, followed by verb, undergoer, and location. The brackets identify semantic functions whose order changes while their relations to the eating event remain constant.

pages.title: What functional planning has established
pages.c: **Functional planning establishes lexical choices and their relations within the intended event.** A message has been selected, appropriate lemmas have been chosen, and those lemmas have been associated with semantic roles. This creates an organized basis for a sentence without yet specifying a complete spoken clause.
support: For an eating event, the system can identify EAT, the participant acting, and the thing being eaten. These choices do not by themselves determine whether the sentence will be active or passive, how the pronouns will be expressed, or the complete sound sequence.
Separating these achievements explains how a lexical choice can move or change while later processes still impose grammatical organization on the resulting utterance.
pages.d: The functional representation contains more than a collection of unrelated words. It connects chosen lexical identities through their roles in a message. The additional work of ordering and expressing those identities is what turns this organized plan into a particular sentence.

pages.title: Errors, interpretation, and deliberate humor
pages.c: **An unusual expression can result from an unnoticed error or a deliberate stylistic choice.** Listeners often use context and expectations to recover an intended message despite imperfect wording. The same top-down influences that support understanding can also make a speaker’s actual error less noticeable.
support: “The upper hand is on the other foot” deliberately combines familiar expressions. Recognizing “the upper hand” and the idea that the shoe is on the other foot makes the odd combination interpretable and humorous.

The conspicuous mismatch can draw attention to the wording itself. This differs from a slip that passes unnoticed because the listener concentrates on the expected message. Whether the expression was intentional matters when using it as evidence about spontaneous production.
pages.d: Context can pull attention toward the intended meaning, allowing irregular wording to pass. Deliberate humor can instead make that wording the point of the utterance. The relation between familiar expressions helps the listener recognize both what is meant and why the form is unusual.
pages.visual: The quotation “The upper hand is on the other foot” places parts of two familiar idioms in one expression. Its humor depends on recognizing the contributing phrases, rather than treating the literal body-part arrangement as the intended event.

questions.stem: A speaker accidentally uses a sound from the next word. Which source of activation most directly explains the sound’s availability?
choices: Material already being prepared for an upcoming part of the utterance.
Only the acoustic echo of material spoken several sentences earlier.
An absence of activation for all words except the current one.
The listener’s decision about where the current word ends.
questions.why: Upcoming material is already active during planning. That overlap makes anticipation possible.

questions.stem: In the contraband tip-of-the-tongue example, which prime condition produces the highest recovery rate?
choices: Words sharing the target’s first syllable.
Words sharing only the target’s final syllable.
Words unrelated to the target’s sound form.
Every condition produces the same recovery rate.
questions.why: First-syllable primes produce the tallest bar, at about 50 percent resolution. The comparison links recovery to the location of phonological overlap.

questions.stem: The intended “John gave the boy” becomes “John gave the goy.” What kind of error is this?
choices: Perseveration, because an earlier g carries into a later position.
Anticipation, because the g first occurs after the changed word.
Metathesis, because the two initial consonants trade positions.
A mondegreen, because a listener changes the word boundaries.
questions.why: The g in gave precedes boy in the intended expression. Its influence persists into the later word, and the original g remains in place.

questions.stem: Why is hearing “laid him on the green” as “Lady Mondegreen” informative about perception?
choices: The listener assigns continuous speech to different words and boundaries.
The speaker has exchanged two fully specified lemmas.
The listener has retained all the original word boundaries unchanged.
The speaker has necessarily failed to articulate any consonants.
questions.why: The mishearing concerns the listener’s segmentation and lexical interpretation of the spoken expression.

questions.stem: A person intentionally says “congenial heart defect” after learning the phrase that way. Which account fits the example?
choices: A similar familiar word was accepted during perception and later repeated as intended.
The person necessarily selected congenital correctly and exchanged two consonants during articulation.
The expression demonstrates that congenial and congenital have identical meanings.
A final-syllable prime deliberately induced a tip-of-the-tongue state.
questions.why: The example distinguishes an intended repetition of a misinterpreted expression from an unplanned production slip.

questions.stem: Why does “fish grotto” becoming “frish gotto” support segment-sized planning units?
choices: The r leaves the gr cluster while g remains, so the cluster is not moved as a whole.
Both complete initial clusters exchange without any internal change.
The two nouns exchange their positions in the sentence.
The error preserves the entire gr cluster in its original word.
questions.why: The changed cluster structure is the critical evidence. A whole-cluster exchange would carry g together with r, while this error moves r by itself.

questions.stem: What is the key evidence for lemmas in “Where’d I put it when I brought it in” becoming “Where’d I bring it when I put it in”?
choices: BRING moves to a new position and receives the form appropriate after did.
The unchanged surface word brought moves intact into the first clause.
Both verbs lose all grammatical properties and become nouns.
The verb put visibly changes from a past form to a different base form.
questions.why: The lexical identity BRING exchanges, but bring rather than brought appears after the auxiliary. This separates lexical selection from final grammatical form.

questions.stem: Why can an antonym be an effective competitor during lemma selection?
choices: It shares a semantic domain and often grammatical roles with the intended item.
It is unrelated in meaning and cannot occupy the same sentence position.
Its selection always requires replacing the complete sentence structure.
Opposite meanings prevent activation from spreading between the words.
questions.why: Antonyms combine semantic relation, association, and grammatical compatibility. A substitution can reverse the message while preserving a well-formed sentence.

questions.stem: How does the produced blend “swindged” differ from a word exchange?
choices: Material from two lexical alternatives contributes to one output form.
Two complete words trade positions without any change to their forms.
Only the listener changes a boundary between two spoken words.
The speaker repeats a correctly selected word with its original sound form.
questions.why: Phonological material associated with the competing verbs SWITCH and CHANGE appears in one blended form rather than as two exchanged words.

questions.stem: What remains stable between “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me” and “I have eaten the plums in the icebox”?
choices: The speaker is the agent and the plums are the undergoer.
The first noun phrase is the agent in both sentences.
The speaker’s pronoun has the same surface form in both sentences.
The agent follows the verb in both sentences.
questions.why: Semantic roles describe participation in the eating event. The active and passive sentences change order and pronoun form while preserving those roles.

written.prompt: Use “fish grotto” becoming “frish gotto” to explain how a speech error can distinguish planning units. Compare the observed form with the whole-cluster alternative.
answer: The observed form moves r out of gr and attaches it to f. The g remains in the second word, so the initial cluster has been separated.

If f and gr exchanged as indivisible clusters, gr would move together to the first word and f would begin the second. The observed separation of r from g supports a representation that allows individual consonants to participate in planning.

written.prompt: Explain what the put and bring exchange reveals about lemmas, then relate this distinction to the active and passive plum sentences.
answer: BRING exchanges positions with PUT, but its new position after did calls for bring rather than brought. Lexical selection is therefore distinguishable from the final grammatical form.

In the plum sentences, the speaker remains the agent and the plums the undergoer while their order and grammatical expression change. Functional planning associates lemmas with semantic roles before the complete sentence form is settled.
